<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
We call a $p$-adic height {\it supported at $p$} if all the local height contributions at the primes of bad reduction are zero.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main1}
Let $N>714$ be squarefree and $p\nmid N$ a prime. Then there exists a $p$-adic height on $X_0(N)^*$ that is supported at $p$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main1.1}
Let $N$ be squarefree and $p\nmid N$ a prime. Then the number of linearly independent $p$-adic heights supported at $p$ on $X_0(N)^*$ is at least $g(X_0(N)^*)-O(\sqrt N\log N$), with an absolute implied constant. In particular, for every $\varepsilon>0$ it is at least $N^{1-\varepsilon}$ for all sufficiently large $N$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:main2}
Let $N$ be an integer and $\ell$ be a prime that exactly divides $N$. Assume that $X_0(N)^*$ has genus at least $2$. Then the curve $X_0(N)^*$ is stable over ${\mathbf{Z}}_\ell$, and hence its minimal regular model is semi-stable.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:correspondence_algorithm}
Let $N$ be a squarefree integer, put $g\colonequals g(X_0(N)^*)$, and let $\mathbb T\subseteq \End \, J_0(N)^*$ be the Hecke algebra generated by the Hecke operators $T_q$ with $q\nmid N$. Let $p\nmid N$ be a prime such that $T_p$ generates $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$ as a ${\mathbf{Q}}$-algebra. Then there exists an algorithm that takes $N$ and $p$ as input, and outputs a sequence of polynomials $f_1,\ldots,f_n\in{\mathbf{Q}}[x]$ of degree at most $g-1$, with $n\geqslant g-1-\sum_{\ell\mid N}L_\ell(N)$, where $L_\ell(N)$ is the number of ``long loops'' (see~\Cref{def:L_ell}), such that the $p$-adic heights associated to the correspondences $f_1(T_p),\ldots,f_n(T_p)$ are linearly independent $p$-adic heights supported at $p$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:examples}
Let $N=187,247$ or $319$. Then the ${\mathbf{Q}}$-rational points on $X_0(N)^*$ are cusps or CM-points.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
There exist at least $\rho(X)-1 - \sum_{\ell}(C_\ell-1)$ linearly independent $p$-adic heights on $X$ supported at $p$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The height contribution on the component containing $b_{{\mathbf{F}}_\ell}$ is zero by definition, and every other component forces a linear condition on the height in order for the height contribution at $\ell$ to vanish on that component. In particular, the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:small_lie}
    Actually, different components over ${\mathbf{F}}_\ell$ of the minimal regular model of $X_0(N)^*$ might impose the same linear condition on the height function. This happens often in practice. Indeed, the dual graph of $X_0(N)^*$ is a single central vertex with several loops attached to it. And all components lying on the same loop impose the same linear condition (\Cref{lem:quadratic_along_edge}). In our actual proof, we replace $C_\ell-1$ by a slightly smaller integer $L_\ell$, the number of loops of the dual graph containing at least one component of the minimal regular model, i.e.\ the number of all loops of length $>1$. However, this is just an optimisation to get slightly better bounds, and not something that is essential to the core idea of the argument.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:thickness}
Let $R$ be a DVR with closed point $s \in \Spec R$. Let $X \to \Spec R$ be a semi-stable curve, and let
$x \in X_s$ be an ordinary double point lying above a prime $s$.
Étale locally at $x$ (possibly after passing to a finite étale extension of
$\Spec R$), the completed local ring has the form
\[
\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{X,x} \cong
\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{R,s}\llbracket u,v \rrbracket/(uv-c),
\]
                            
for some $c \in M_s$ (maximal ideal of the local ring).
The \emph{thickness} $i_x$ of $x$ is defined as
$i_x \colonequals v_s(c)$ with respect to the normalized valuation of
$\mathcal{O}_{R,s}$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:regual_from_semistable_model}
Let $R$ be a DVR with closed point $s$.    Let $X \to \Spec R$ be a semi-stable projective curve 
with smooth generic fibre $X_\eta$. Let $\pi\colon X' \to X$ be the minimal desingularisation, 
$x \in X_s$ a split ordinary double point, of thickness $i$ in $X$. Then $\pi^{-1}(x)$ is 
made up of a chain of $i-1$ projective lines over $k(s)$ that meet transversally at rational 
points. These lines are of multiplicity $1$ in $X_s'$, and have self-intersection $-2$ in $X'$. (For a picture, see~\cite[Figure 48]{Liu2002}.)
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
See~\cite[Corollary 10.3.25]{Liu2002}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:minimal_regular_from_stable_model}
    Let $\mathcal X$ be a stable model over a discrete valuation ring $R$. Let $K$ be the field of fractions of $R$ and $X := \mathcal X_K$. Let $\mathcal X'$ be the minimal desingularisation of $\mathcal X$. Then $\mathcal X'$ is a minimal regular model of $\mathcal X$, and in particular $\mathcal X'$ is semi-stable.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The proof follows the proof in \cite[Theorem 10.3.34(a)]{Liu2002}. In that proof the minimal regular model is obtained from a semi-stable model by first passing to the minimal desingularisation and then contracting all chains of ${\mathbf{P}}^1$'s that meet the other irreducible components in just a single point. However, a stable model does not have any chain of ${\mathbf{P}}^1$'s that meet the other components in a single point. And furthermore in the minimal desingularisation of a stable model, there are no chains of ${\mathbf{P}}^1$'s that meet the other components in just a single point. As the only chains of ${\mathbf{P}}^1$'s that are introduced in this desingularisation process are chain's of ${\mathbf{P}}^1$'s that connect two points by \Cref{cor:regual_from_semistable_model}. This implies that $\mathcal X'$ is the minimal regular model. That $\mathcal X'$ is semi-stable is the content of  \cite[Theorem 10.3.34(a)]{Liu2002}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:reduction_graph}
Let $X$ be a nice curve over ${\mathbf{Q}}_\ell$ of genus $\geqslant 2$. Let $K/{\mathbf{Q}}_\ell$ be a finite extension of ramification index $r$ over which $X/{\mathbf{Q}}_\ell$ acquires semi-stable reduction. Let $\mathcal X/\mathcal{O}_K$ be a semi-stable model $X$ and write its special fibre $\mathcal X_s=\bigcup_w X_w$ as a union of its irreducible components. The \emph{dual graph} (or \emph{reduction graph}) $\mathcal{G}$ of $\mathcal X$ has one vertex $w\in V(\mathcal{G})$ for each irreducible component $X_w$ of $\mathcal X_s$ and one edge $e\in E(\mathcal{G})$ for each ordinary double point, joining the two components meeting there. An ordinary double point of thickness $i_e$ (\Cref{def:thickness}) is assigned \emph{length} $l(e)=i_e/r$. We write $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{Q}}$ for the set of points of the resulting metric graph lying at rational distance from a vertex (the points with coordinate \(x_e \in {\mathbf{Q}} \cap [0, l(e)]\) on some edge $e$), and similarly $\mathcal{G}_{\frac 1r {\mathbf{Z}}}$ for those points that lie on a distance of length $\frac 1r {\mathbf{Z}}$ away from a vertex.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:reduction_map}
Let $X$ be a curve over ${\mathbf{Q}}_\ell$ that acquires semi-stable reduction over a field extension $K$ of ${\mathbf{Q}}_\ell$ of ramification index $r$ and let $\mathcal X'$ be a regular semi-stable model of $X$. The \emph{reduction map} $\mathrm{red}\colon X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)\to \mathcal{G}_{\frac 1r {\mathbf{Z}}}$ is defined to be the map that sends a point to the component of $\mathcal X'_s$ to which it reduces.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:cycle_space}
Orient the edges and let ${\mathbf{Q}}\,E(\mathcal{G})$ be the ${\mathbf{Q}}$-vector space on them, with the pairing $e\cdot e'=\delta_{ee'}\,l(e)$ given by the lengths. Inside it sits the \emph{cycle space} $\mathrm{H}_1(\mathcal{G},{\mathbf{Q}})=\ker\left(\partial\colon{\mathbf{Q}}\,E(\mathcal{G})\to{\mathbf{Q}}\,V(\mathcal{G})\right)$, the first homology of $\mathcal{G}$. Let $\pi\colon{\mathbf{Q}}\,E(\mathcal{G})\to\mathrm{H}_1(\mathcal{G},{\mathbf{Q}})$ be the orthogonal projection for this pairing and $e^*\colon{\mathbf{Q}}\,E(\mathcal{G})\to{\mathbf{Q}}$ the coordinate functional dual to $e$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:pp_measure}
A continuous function $g\colon\mathcal{G} \to{\mathbf{R}}$ is \emph{piecewise polynomial} if $g_e$ is a polynomial for every edge $e$. A \emph{piecewise polynomial measure} on $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{Q}}$ is a formal sum
\[
  \mu=\sum_{e\in E(\mathcal{G})}\mu_e\cdot\lvert\mathrm{d}x_e\rvert+\sum_{w\in V(\mathcal{G})}\mu_w\cdot\delta_w ,
\]
in which each $\mu_e$ is a polynomial in $x_e$ and each $\mu_w$ lies in ${\mathbf{R}}$. Here $\lvert\mathrm{d}x_e\rvert$ denotes the Lebesgue measure on $e$, and $\delta_w$ the Dirac measure at $w$. The \emph{total mass} of $\mu$ is
\[
  \lvert \mu\rvert\colonequals\sum_{e\in E(\mathcal{G})}\int_0^{l(e)}\mu_e\,\mathrm{d}x_e+\sum_{w\in V(\mathcal{G})}\mu_w .
\]
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:graph_laplacian}
Let $g\colon\mathcal{G} \to {\mathbf{R}}$ be piecewise polynomial. Its \emph{Laplacian} is the piecewise polynomial measure
\[
  \nabla^2(g)\colonequals-\sum_{e\in E(\mathcal{G})}(g_e)''\cdot\lvert\mathrm{d}x_e\rvert-\sum_{w\in V(\mathcal{G})}\sigma_w(g)\cdot\delta_w,
\]
\[ \text{where } \quad \sigma_w(g)\colonequals\sum_{s(e)=w}(g_e)'(0)-\sum_{t(e)=w}(g_e)'\left(l(e)\right),\] and $(g_e)''$ is the second derivative with respect to $x_e$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:CGheight}
    The \emph{\(p \)-adic height pairing} is a symmetric bi-additive pairing
    \(h:\Div^0(X) \times \Div^0(X) \to {\mathbf{Q}}_p\), \((D_1, D_2) \mapsto h(D_1, D_2),\)
for \(D_1, D_2\) divisors of degree \(0\) with disjoint support, such that:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We have
    \[ h(D_1, D_2) = \sum_{v} h_v(D_1, D_2) = h_p(D_1, D_2) + \sum_{\ell\neq p} h_\ell(D_1, D_2),\]
    where \(h_p\) can be expressed via Coleman integral, the sum goes over all primes \(\ell\neq p\) of bad reduction for \(X\), and \(h_\ell(D_1, D_2)=m_\ell \chi_\ell(\ell\)), where \(m_\ell\in {\mathbf{Q}}\) can be defined in terms of intersection theory \cite[Equation (1.3)]{ColemanGross}.
    \item We have \(h(D, \div(f))=0\) for all \(f\in {\mathbf{Q}}(X)^*\).
\end{enumerate}
By \((ii)\), \(h\) induces a symmetric bilinear pairing \(J({\mathbf{Q}}) \times J({\mathbf{Q}}) \to {\mathbf{Q}}_p\).
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:padic_height} Let $b \in X({\mathbf{Q}})$ be a basepoint and $Z \otimes a \in \NS(J(X)) \otimes {\mathbf{Q}}$ be a correspondence of trace $0$. Then the {\it $p$-adic height associated to $Z \otimes a$} is the function $h_{Z,b}\colon X({\mathbf{Q}})\to{\mathbf{Q}}_p$ given by
\begin{align*}
   h_{Z,b} :   X({\mathbf{Q}}) &\to{\mathbf{Q}}_p \\
    z &\mapsto ah(z-b,D_Z(b,z)).
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:linear_independence}The height from \Cref{def:padic_height} is in terms of the Coleman-Gross height from \Cref{def:CGheight}, and hence also depends on a character $\chi : {\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbf{Q}}^\times \to {\mathbf{Q}}_p$ and a splitting of the Hodge filtration. Changing $\chi$ only changes each local height $h_{\ell}$ by a multiplicative constant. Changing the splitting of the Hodge filtration only changes the local height at $p$. In particular, whether $p$-adic height is supported at $p$ does not depend on these choices. Hence, after having fixed a basepoint, it is safe to think of these $p$-adic heights as being parametrised by the vector space of trace $0$ elements in $\NS(J(X)) \otimes {\mathbf{Q}}$. In particular, the linear independence statement from \Cref{thm:main1.1} should be interpreted as taking place in $(\NS(J(X)) \otimes {\mathbf{Q}})^{\operatorname{tr}=0}$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
A trace zero correspondence $Z$ on a curve $X$ over ${\mathbf{Q}}$ is called a {\it{clean correspondence}} if $h_{Z,b}$ is a $p$-adic height supported at $p$, i.e.\ if the local contributions $h_\ell$ to $h_{Z,b}$ mentioned above are zero for all primes $\ell \neq p$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
The function $\rho_{Z,b} := h_B - h_p :X({\mathbf{Q}}_p) \to {\mathbf{Q}}_p$ is called the \emph{quadratic Chabauty function} associated to the divisor $Z$ and basepoint $b$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\cite[Thm 1.2]{BalakrishnanDogra1}
Assume that $X$ is a nice curve over ${\mathbf{Q}}$, $Z$ a trace  correspondence on $X$, $b \in X({\mathbf{Q}})$ a basepoint and $p$ a prime of good reduction for $X$. Then one has that $\rho_{Z,b}(X({\mathbf{Q}})) \subseteq \Upsilon$. Furthermore $\rho_{Z,b}^{-1}(\Upsilon)$ is a finite subset of $X({\mathbf{Q}}_p)$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:corr_endomorphism}
Let $Z$ be a a trace 0 correspondence. Then the endomorphism $F_Z$ of $\mathrm{H}_1(\mathcal{G},{\mathbf{Q}})$ and $\mathrm{H}_1(\mathcal{G},{\mathbf{Q}})\otimes {\mathbf{Q}}_p$, $\bigoplus_{w\in V(\mathcal{G})}V_p(X_w)$ are defined to be those induced by the action of $Z$ on the graded pieces of $V_p(X)$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:corr_measure}
The \emph{measure} of the endomorphism $F := F_Z$ of \Cref{def:corr_endomorphism} is
\[
  \mu_F=\sum_{e\in E(\mathcal{G})}\frac{1}{l(e)}\,e^*F\left(\pi(e)\right)\cdot \lvert\mathrm{d}x_e\rvert+\tfrac12\sum_{w\in V(\mathcal{G})}\operatorname{Tr}\left(F\mid V_p(X_w)\right)\cdot \delta_w ,
\]
with $\pi$ and $e^*$ as in \Cref{def:cycle_space}.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:measure_subdivision}
The measure $\mu_F$ is invariant under subdivision of the underlying metric graph: if $\mathcal{G}'$ is obtained from $\mathcal{G}$ by subdividing an edge $e$ into edges $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of lengths $l_1,\dots,l_n$, the new vertices carrying rational components, then $\mu_{F'}=\mu_F$ under the identification $\mathcal{G}'_{\mathbf{Q}}=\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{Q}}$. Indeed, $\pi'(e_i)=\tfrac{l_i}{l(e)}\,\pi(e)$, so the edge densities $\tfrac{1}{l(e_i)}\,e_i^*F\left(\pi'(e_i)\right)=\tfrac{1}{l(e)}\,e^*F\left(\pi(e)\right)$ agree, and the new vertices contribute nothing, see also \Cref{lem:measure_subdivision} in the Appendix.
Moreover, \Cref{lem:laplacian_mass,lem:measure_mass} (from the Appendix) say that the equation $\nabla^2(g)=\mu_F$ of \Cref{thm:BDMTV_localheight} below is solvable \emph{precisely} when $F$ has trace $0$ on $\mathrm H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X_{{\mathbf{Q}}_\ell})$, and that its solution is then unique up to a constant, which the normalisation at $\mathrm{red}(b)$ removes.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:BDMTV_localheight}
Keep the notation of \Cref{def:reduction_graph,def:cycle_space,def:pp_measure,def:graph_laplacian,def:corr_measure} and fix a basepoint $b\in X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$. Then the local height factors through reduction to the graph,
\[
  h_\ell=\kappa\cdot j_\mathcal{G}\circ\mathrm{red}\colon X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)\longrightarrow{\mathbf{Q}}_p,
\]
for a nonzero constant $\kappa \in {\mathbf{Q}}_p$ independent of the point, where $j_\mathcal{G}\colon\mathcal{G}\to{\mathbf{R}}$ is the unique piecewise-quadratic function determined by
\[
  j_\mathcal{G}\left(\mathrm{red}(b)\right)=0,\qquad \nabla^2(j_\mathcal{G})=\mu_F .
\]
In particular $h_\ell$ is locally constant, its value depends only on the component to which the point reduces, and it attains only finitely many values.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Note that the function $j_\mathcal{G}$ is a priori only a real-valued function and there is no well defined way to multiply elements of ${\mathbf{R}}$ with $\kappa \in {\mathbf{Q}}_p$. For the theorem above this is not a problem however as we will shortly explain. Indeed, if $X$ attains semi-stable reduction over a field extension $K$ of ${\mathbf{Q}}_\ell$ of ramification index $r$ then $\mathrm{red}$ only takes values in the finite set $\mathcal{G}_{\frac 1r  {\mathbf{Z}}}$, the subset of points in $\mathcal{G}$ whose distance to a vertex lies in  $\frac 1r {\mathbf{Z}}$. And on this subset of points (in fact on the larger set of points $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{Q}}$) one can show that $j_\mathcal{G}$ only takes on ${\mathbf{Q}}$-rational values. So $j_\mathcal{G} \circ \mathrm{red}$ takes values in ${\mathbf{Q}}$, and after embedding ${\mathbf{Q}}$ in ${\mathbf{Q}}_p$ it makes sense to multiply it with $\kappa$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:quadratic_along_edge}
Let $\mathcal{G}$ be the dual graph of a semi-stable model of $X$ at $\ell$ (\Cref{def:reduction_graph}), let $F$ be an endomorphism as in \Cref{def:corr_endomorphism}, let $\mu_F$ be its measure (\Cref{def:corr_measure}) and let $g\colon\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{Q}}\to{\mathbf{Q}}_p$ be a continuous piecewise polynomial function with $\nabla^2(g)=\mu_F$ (\Cref{def:graph_laplacian}). Let $e\in E(\mathcal{G})$ be an edge, put $l\colonequals l(e)$ and identify $e$ with the interval $[0,l]$ by arclength, the point $0$ being the source $s(e)$ and the point $l$ the target $t(e)$. Assume that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item every vertex lying in the interior of $e$ in the subdivision of $\mathcal{G}$ induced by the minimal regular model corresponds to a component of the special fibre of genus $0$, and
    \item the edge part of $\mu_F$ has constant density $c\in{\mathbf{Q}}_p$ along $e$.
\end{enumerate}
Set $a\colonequals g(s(e))$ and $b\colonequals g(t(e))$. Then
\[
    g(x)\;=\;a\;+\;(b-a)\,\frac{x}{l}\;-\;\frac{c}{2}\,x\,(x-l)
    \qquad\text{for all }x\in[0,l].
\]
In particular, if $a=b=0$, then $g_e(x)=-\tfrac{c}{2}\,x\,(x-l)$, which vanishes identically if $c=0$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Subdividing $e$ into segments $[x_{i-1},x_i]$, $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$, with $0=x_0<x_1<\dots<x_n=l$, changes neither $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{Q}}$ nor $g$, and it does not change $\mu_F$ by \Cref{rem:measure_subdivision}; we may therefore compute with the subdivision. Write $w_i$ for the interior vertex sitting at $x_i$, $1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$. Each $w_i$ has degree $2$, the two segments meeting there being $[x_{i-1},x_i]$ and $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$.

Comparing the coefficients of the segment $[x_{i-1},x_i]$ in $\nabla^2(g)=\mu_F$ gives, by \Cref{def:graph_laplacian} and assumption~(ii), the identity $g''=-c$ on $(x_{i-1},x_i)$. As $g$ is polynomial there, $g|_{[x_{i-1},x_i]}$ has degree at most $2$ with leading coefficient $-c/2$.

Comparing the coefficients of the vertex $w_i$ gives that the sum of the outgoing slopes of $g$ at $w_i$ equals $-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(F\mid V_p(X_{w_i}))$. By assumption~(i) the component $X_{w_i}$ has genus $0$, so its Jacobian is trivial, $V_p(X_{w_i})=0$, and this trace vanishes. In the coordinate $x$ the two outgoing slopes of $g$ at $w_i$ are $-g'(x_i^-)$ and $g'(x_i^+)$, so their sum being $0$ means precisely that the two one-sided derivatives of $g$ at $x_i$ agree.

Hence $h(x)\colonequals g(x)+\tfrac{c}{2}x^2$ is continuous on $[0,l]$, is affine on each segment $[x_{i-1},x_i]$, and has matching one-sided derivatives at $x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}$; therefore $h$ is affine on all of $[0,l]$ and $g_e(x)=-\tfrac{c}{2}x^2+\beta x+\gamma$ for some $\beta,\gamma\in{\mathbf{Q}}_p$. Evaluating at $x=0$ gives $\gamma=a$, and evaluating at $x=l$ gives $b=-\tfrac{c}{2}l^2+\beta l+a$, i.e.\ $\beta=\tfrac{b-a}{l}+\tfrac{c\,l}{2}$. Substituting these two values yields the displayed formula.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:quaternion_algebra}
A \emph{quaternion algebra} $B$ over a field $F$ is a four-dimensional central simple algebra over $F$. It is \emph{split} over $F$ if $B\cong M_2(F)$. If $\operatorname{char} F\neq 2$ and $a,b\in F^\times$, we denote by $\left(\frac{a,b}{F}\right)$ the quaternion algebra $F \oplus F i \oplus F j \oplus F k$ with multiplication given by $i^2 = a$, $j^2 = b$ and $k = ij = -ji$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def:ramification}
Let $B$ be a quaternion algebra over a global field $F$. For a place $v$ of $F$, put $B_v\colonequals B\otimes_F F_v$. The \emph{ramification set} $\Ram(B)$ is the set of places $v$ of $F$ such that $B_v$ is a division algebra. If $F={\mathbf{Q}}$, the product $D$ of the primes in $\Ram(B)$ is called the \emph{discriminant} of $B$, and $B$ is called \emph{definite} if $\infty\in\Ram(B)$.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:ramification_set}
For every quaternion algebra $B$ over ${\mathbf{Q}}$, the set $\Ram(B)$ is a finite set of places of ${\mathbf{Q}}$ of even cardinality. Conversely, every finite set of places of ${\mathbf{Q}}$ of even cardinality is $\Ram(B)$ for some quaternion algebra $B$ over ${\mathbf{Q}}$, unique up to isomorphism.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
See \cite[p.~452, Proof of Main Theorem 14.6.1]{Voight2021}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{def:order}
An \emph{order} $\mathcal{O}$ in a quaternion algebra $B$ over ${\mathbf{Q}}$ is a subring of $B$ (with $1$) that is a lattice, i.e., a finitely generated ${\mathbf{Z}}$-submodule of rank $4$. An order is \emph{maximal} if it is not properly contained in any other order of $B$. Orders in quaternion algebras over ${\mathbf{Q}}_q$ are defined in the same way, with ${\mathbf{Z}}_q$ in place of ${\mathbf{Z}}$. For an order $\mathcal{O}$ in $B$, its completion $\mathcal{O}_q\colonequals\mathcal{O}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}{\mathbf{Z}}_q$ is an order in $B\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}{\mathbf{Q}}_q$.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{def:eichler_order}
An \emph{Eichler order} is the intersection of two maximal orders, which includes the maximal orders themselves. In the split quaternion algebra over \({\mathbf{Q}}_q\), every Eichler order is conjugate to \( \big(\begin{smallmatrix} {\mathbf{Z}}_q  & {\mathbf{Z}}_q  \\ q^e {\mathbf{Z}}_q  & {\mathbf{Z}}_q \end{smallmatrix}\big)\), the \emph{standard Eichler order of level} \(q^e \), where $e\geqslant 0$.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{def:eichler_level}
Let $B$ be a quaternion algebra over ${\mathbf{Q}}$ of discriminant $D$, and let $M$ be a positive integer coprime to $D$. An order $\mathcal{O}$ in $B$ is an \emph{Eichler order of level} $M$ if, for every prime $q\mid M$, the completion $\mathcal{O}_q$ is isomorphic to the standard Eichler order of level $q^e$, where $q^e\parallel M$, and $\mathcal{O}_q$ is maximal for every prime $q\nmid M$.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
A ${\mathbf{Z}}$-lattice $I\subset B$ is a \emph{right $\mathcal{O}$-ideal} if $I\mathcal{O}=I$. It is \emph{invertible} (equivalently, \emph{locally principal}) if for every prime $q$ we have $I \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} {\mathbf{Z}}_q = \alpha_q \mathcal{O}_q$ for $\alpha_q \in B_q^\times$. The \emph{left order} of $I$ is \(
  O_L(I)\colonequals\{\,x\in B : xI\subseteq I\,\},
\)
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\label{def:class_set}
Two invertible right $\mathcal{O}$-ideals $I, J$ are \emph{equivalent} if $J=\alpha I$ for some $\alpha \in B^\times$. The \emph{class set} $\operatorname{Cls}\mathcal{O}$ is the set of equivalence classes $[I]$ of invertible right $\mathcal{O}$-ideals, and $\#\operatorname{Cls}\mathcal{O}$ is the \emph{class number} of $\mathcal{O}$.
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{def:splitting_symbol}
Let $K$ be a quadratic field, $q$ a prime, and $K_q\colonequals K\otimes_{\mathbf{Q}}{\mathbf{Q}}_q$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pInK}
\left(\frac{K}{q}\right) \colonequals
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if $q$ splits in $K$, i.e., } K_q \cong{\mathbf{Q}}_q\times{\mathbf{Q}}_q;\\
0, & \text{if $q$ ramifies in $K$;}\\
-1, & \text{if $q$ is inert in $K$.}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{def:embedding_number}
Let $\mathcal{O}$  be an order in a quaternion algebra $B$ over ${\mathbf{Q}}$, and let $S$ be an order in a quadratic field $K$. We denote by $m(S, \mathcal{O})$ the number of $\mathcal{O}^\times$-conjugacy classes of optimal embeddings $S\hookrightarrow\mathcal{O}$.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{O} \subset B$ be an Eichler order of squarefree level $M$, and $D = \operatorname{disc} B$, so that $\gcd(D,M)=1$. Let $K$ be an imaginary quadratic field, and let $S\subset K$ be an order that is maximal at every prime dividing $DM$. Denote the class number of $S$ by $h(S)$. Then
\[
\sum_{[I]\in\operatorname{Cls} \mathcal{O}}
   m\left(S,O_L(I)\right)
   \;=\; h(S)\,\prod_{p\mid D}\left(1-\left(\tfrac{K}{p}\right)\right)\,
         \prod_{p\mid M}\left(1+\left(\tfrac{K}{p}\right)\right).
\]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Combine \cite[Theorem~30.4.7]{Voight2021} with the local embedding numbers in \cite[\S\S\,30.5--30.6]{Voight2021}. See also \cite[Example 30.7.5]{Voight2021} for a very similar statement.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:Deuring}
    Let $\ell$ and $M$ be as above.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For every pair $(E, G)$ as above, $\End(E)\otimes {\mathbf{Q}} \cong B_{\ell, \infty}$, the ring $\End(E)$ is a maximal order in it, and $\End(E,G)$ is an Eichler order of level $M$ in it.
        \item Fix a pair $(E_0, G_0)$ as above and put $\mathcal{O}_0 \colonequals \End(E_0, G_0)$. There is a bijection between the isomorphisms classes of pairs $(E, G)$ and $\operatorname{Cls}\mathcal{O}_0$ such that, if $(E,G)$ corresponds to $[I]$, then $\End(E,G)\cong \mathcal{O}_L(I)$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The statements about $\End(E)$ are Deuring's theorem \cite{Deuring1951}, \cite[Theorem 42.1.9]{Voight2021}, and the statement about $\End(E,G)$ is \cite[Theorem 3.7]{Arpin24} (see also \cite[Remark 42.3.10]{Voight2021}). Part~(ii) follows from the equivalence of categories \cite[Theorem 6.5]{Arpin24}, which sends $(E,G)$ to an invertible left $\mathcal{O}_0$-module whose right order is isomorphic to $\End(E,G)$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:lefteqright}
    The standard involution turns left ideal classes into right ideal classes, and right orders into left orders. A reader may find a different convention compared to ours depending on the reference (e.~g.~\cite{Arpin24}).
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:aut_classification}
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over $\overline{{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell $, and let $j(E)$ denote its $j$-invariant. The automorphism group $\Aut(E)$ is given by:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $j(E) \not\equiv 0, 1728 \pmod \ell$, then $\Aut(E) \cong {\mathbf{Z}}/2{\mathbf{Z}}$.
    \item If $j(E) \equiv 1728 \pmod \ell$ and $\ell \neq 2, 3$, then $\Aut(E) \cong {\mathbf{Z}}/4{\mathbf{Z}}$.
    \item If $j(E) \equiv 0 \pmod \ell$ and $\ell \neq 2, 3$, then $\Aut(E) \cong {\mathbf{Z}}/6{\mathbf{Z}}$.
    \item If $\ell = 3$ and $j(E) \equiv 0 \equiv 1728 \pmod 3$, then $\Aut(E) \cong {\mathbf{Z}}/3{\mathbf{Z}} \rtimes {\mathbf{Z}}/4{\mathbf{Z}}$.
    \item If $\ell = 2$ and $j(E) \equiv 0 \equiv 1728 \pmod 2$, then $\Aut(E) \cong \SL_2({\mathbf{F}}_3)$.
\end{enumerate}
where the action of ${\mathbf{Z}}/4{\mathbf{Z}}$ on ${\mathbf{Z}}/3{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the unique nontrivial action, and the isomorphism  $\Aut(E) \cong \SL_2( {\mathbf{F}}_3)$ comes from the action of $\Aut(E)$ on $E[3](\overline{{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell )$
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
This is Proposition 4.4 from \cite{Schoof87}, who references \cite[p. 182]{Tate78} and Deuring \cite[\S\,5]{Deuring41}. The same statement just mentioning the group order is also in \cite[Theorem~III.10.1]{Silverman1}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- setup-1: body_md -->
\label{setup:al_quotient} Let $\ell$ be a prime and $M$ be an integer (not necessarily squarefree) coprime to $\ell$ and $N \colonequals \ell M$ and $W \subseteq W_N$ a subgroup of the Atkin--Lehner operators on $X_0(N)$.
<!-- end setup-1 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prop:semi-stable_quotient}
Let $S$ be the spectrum of a discrete valuation ring $R$ with closed point $s$. 
Let $X$ be a semi-stable quasi-projective curve over $S$, endowed with 
the action of a finite group $G$. Then the quotient scheme 
$Y = X/G$ is semi-stable. More precisely, let $x \in X_s$ be a closed 
point, $y$ its image in $Y_s$. Then we have the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item if $X$ is smooth at $x$, then $Y$ is smooth at $y$;
    \item if $x$ is an ordinary double point of $X_s$, then $y$ is a 
    smooth or ordinary double point; 
    \item let $I'$ be the image of the inertia group $I$ at $x$ in 
    $\mathrm{Aut}_R(\mathcal{O}_{X,x})$. If $x$ is split of 
    thickness $m$, and if $y$ is a double point, then $y$ is split of 
    thickness $mn$, where $n$ is the order of $I'$.
    \item If $x$ is an ordinary double point then $y$ is a smooth point if and only if there is an element $\iota$ in the inertia group $I$ at $x$ that swaps the two components at $x$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Items $(i), (ii)$ and $(iii)$ are~\cite[Proposition~10.3.48]{Liu2002}. The fourth item follows from the proof of \cite[Proposition~10.3.48]{Liu2002}. Indeed, let $I_0$ be the subgroup of elements of $I$ that do not swap the two branches. Then the proof of \cite[Proposition~10.3.48]{Liu2002} contains a case distinction based on whether $I=I_0$, or not. In the case $I=I_0$ one has that $y$ is an ordinary double point and in the case $I \neq I_0$ one has that $y$ is a smooth point.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label[theorem]{thm:semi-stable_X0} Let $\ell, M$ and $N$ be as in \cref{setup:al_quotient}. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The curve model $X_0(N)_{{\mathbf{Z}}[1/M]}$ is a semi-stable curve over $\Spec{\mathbf{Z}}[1/M]$ that is smooth outside of the supersingular points in characteristic $\ell$.
\item $X_0(N)_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell}$ is a curve consisting of two copies of $X_0(M)_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell}$ (corresponding to the kernel of Frobenius and Verschiebung in characteristic $\ell$, respectively) glued transversally together along the supersingular points, where a supersingular point $x \in X_0(M)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$ on the first copy is identified with $\operatorname{Frob}_\ell  x$ on the second copy of $X_0(M)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$. The two components are the images of the degeneracy maps $(E,G)\mapsto(E,G)$ and $(E,G)\mapsto(E/E[\ell],\,(H+E[\ell])/E[\ell])$. An element $w_d$ swaps the two components if and only if $\ell \mid d$.
\item If $(E,G)$ represents a supersingular point $x\in X_0(N)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$, then the thickness of $x$ equals $\frac 1 2 \#\Aut(E, G)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
This follows from~\cite[Theorem~VI.6.9]{DeRa} and~\cite[Theorem~13.4.7]{KatzMazur} (applied to the étale base change $X_0(M) \to X(1)$ over ${\mathbf{Z}}[1/M]$). Note for~(ii) that from the moduli description, $w_d$ swaps kernel of Frobenius and Verschiebung if and only if $\ell \mid d$. Semistability follows from~(ii) and because $X_0(M)_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell}$ is semi-stable and because the gluing is transversal in the intersection points. For the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in~(iii) note that we always have $[-1] \in \Aut(E,G)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:semi-stable_star}
Let $\ell, M, N$ and $W$ be as in \Cref{setup:al_quotient}. Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item The quotient $(X_0(N)/W)_{{\mathbf{Z}}[1/M]}$ is a semi\-stable curve over $\Spec{\mathbf{Z}}[1/M]$ that is smooth outside of the supersingular points in characteristic $\ell$.

\item Define $W' \colonequals \left\{w_d \in W \middle | \, \ell \nmid d\right\}$. \begin{enumerate}
    \item If $W'\neq W$, then $(X_0(N)/W)_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell }$ consists of a single component isomorphic to $(X_0(M)/W')_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell }$.
    \item  If $W'=W$, then $(X_0(N)/W)_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell }$ has two components, which are both isomorphic to $(X_0(M)/W')_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell }$. 
\end{enumerate}

\item Let $(E,G)$ represent a supersingular point $x\in X_0(N)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell )$ and let $W_x$ be stabiliser of $x$ inside $W$. \begin{enumerate}
    \item If there is an integer $d \mid M$ such that $w_{\ell d} \in W_x$, then $X_0(N)/W$ is smooth at the image of $x$.
    \item If such an integer $d$ does not exist, then $X_0(N)/W$ has an ordinary double point at the image of $x$ whose thickness is $\#W_x \ \frac 1 2 \#\Aut(E, G)$.
\end{enumerate}  
\item Assume $W' \neq W$ and $g((X_0(N)/W)_{\mathbf{Q}}) \geqslant 2$ then it is stable. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
(i) is~\Cref{thm:semi-stable_X0}, and~(ii) follows from it because $w_d$ swaps the two components if and only if $\ell \mid d$.

(iii)\,(a) smoothness: an element $w_{\ell d}\in W_x$ swaps the two branches at the double point (it exchanges the two copies of $X_0(M)$), and a branch-swapping involution folds the double point to a smooth point by \Cref{prop:semi-stable_quotient} (iv).

(iii)\,(b): by~\Cref{prop:semi-stable_quotient}, the thickness is $\#W_x\cdot\tfrac12\#\Aut(E,G)$: this is $mn$ with $m=\tfrac12\#\Aut(E,G)$ and $n=\#W_x$ (note that in case (b) no element of $W_x$ swaps branches) and that $W_x \hookrightarrow I'$ because a nontrivial $w_d$ acting trivially on the local ring would act trivially on the whole $X_0(M)$ component, forcing $d = 1$.

(iv) In this case there is only one component in the special fibre. In particular it is geometrically connected. And since the arithmetic genus of this component is at least $2$, it cannot be (geometrically) isomorphic to ${\mathbf{P}}^1$. Note that the assumption $g((X_0(N)/W)_{\mathbf{Q}})  \geqslant 2$ is needed (rather then merely $\geqslant 1$) as fibres of stable curves need to have arithmetic genus at least $2$ by definition.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:minimal_regular_AL_quot}
Assume $W' \neq W$ and $g((X_0(N)/W)_{\mathbf{Q}})  \geqslant 2$, then the minimal regular model of $X_0(N)/W$ over ${\mathbf{Z}}[1/M]$ is the model obtained by replacing each ordinary double point of $x = (E,G)\in X_0(N)/W$ by a chain of ${\mathbf{P}}^1$-s of length $\#W_x \ \frac 1 2 \#\Aut(E, G)-1$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
This just follows from how the minimal regular model of a stable curve is obtained from a stable model in \Cref{lem:minimal_regular_from_stable_model}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{def:dual_graph_quotient}
    Let $\ell,M,N$ and $W$ be as in \Cref{setup:al_quotient}. Then define the metric graph $\mathcal{G}_W$ as follows:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item if there is an Atkin--Lehner operator in $W$ of the form $w_{\ell d}$ with $d|M$, then $\mathcal{G}_W$ has a single vertex $v_0$. The edges of $\mathcal{G}_W$ correspond to $W$-orbits of supersingular points that are not fixed by Atkin--Lehner operator of the form $w_{\ell d}$. Let $x \in X_0(N)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell )$ be such a point represented by a pair $(E,G)$. Then the edge associated to its $W$-orbit is a loop attached to $v_0$ of length $\#W_x \ \frac 1 2 \#\Aut(E, G)$.
        \item otherwise $\mathcal{G}_W$ has two vertices $v_0, v_1$ with one edge of length $$\#W_x \ \frac 1 2 \#\Aut(E, G)$$ connecting them for each $W$-orbit of supersingular points.
    \end{itemize}
    We use the notation $\mathcal{G}_0(N)$ and $\mathcal{G}_0(N)^*$ when $\#W=1$ and $W=W_N$ the full Atkin--Lehner group, respectively.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:dual_graph_quotient}
    The dual graph of the special fibre over ${\mathbf{F}}_\ell $ of $X_0(N)/W$ is $\mathcal{G}_W$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{def:flower_graph}
A metric graph $\mathcal{G}$ is called a \emph{flower graph} if it has a unique vertex $v_0$, and every edge $e$ of $\mathcal{G}$ is a loop at $v_0$ of integral length.
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- setup-2: body_md -->
\label{setup:al_quotient_hecke} Let $\ell,p$ be distinct primes and $M$ be an integer (not necessarily squarefree) coprime to $\ell$ and $p$. Let $N \colonequals \ell M$ and $W \subseteq W_N$ a subgroup of the Atkin--Lehner operators on $X_0(N)$. We also view $W$ as acting on $X_0(pN)$.
<!-- end setup-2 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
Let $\ell,p, M, N, W$ be as in \Cref{setup:al_quotient_hecke}, and let $Z \subseteq (X_0(N)/W)^2$ be the image of $X_0(pN)$ under $(\iota_1,\iota_2):X_0(pN)/W \to (X_0(N)/W)^2$ then the Hecke operator $T_p$ is defined to be the correspondence induced by $Z$.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:quotient-correspondence}
    Let $K$ be a finite extension of ${\mathbf{Q}}_\ell$ and $X$ and $Y$ be nice curves over $K$. Let $f_1,f_2 : X \to Y$ be finite morphisms, and let $G$ be a group acting faithfully on both $X$ and $Y$ in a way that commutes both with $f_1$ and $f_2$. Let $g_1, g_2 : X/G \to Y/G$ be the morphisms induced by $f_1$ and $f_2$ and $\pi_X :X \to X/G$ and $\pi_Y: Y \to Y/G$ be the quotient maps. Then
    \begin{enumerate}

        \item $\pi_Y^* : H_1(\Gamma_{Y/G}) \to H_1(\Gamma_Y)$ is injective and $\pi_{Y,*}$ is injective when restricted to $\pi_Y^*( H_1(\Gamma_{Y/G}))$.
        \item The endomorphism $f_{2,*}\circ f_1^*$ of $H_1(\Gamma_{Y})\otimes {\mathbf{Q}}$ restricts to a well defined endomorphism of $\pi_Y^*(H_1(\Gamma_{Y/G}) \otimes {\mathbf{Q}})$.
        \item We have $f_{2,*} \circ f_1^* \circ \pi_Y^{*} = \pi_Y^{*} \circ g_{2,*} \circ g_1^*$ in $\Hom(H_1(\Gamma_{Y/G}),H_1(\Gamma_{Y})) $.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
(i) The injectivity follows since $\pi_{Y,*}\circ \pi_Y^*$ is multiplication by $\#G$, and $H_1(\Gamma_{Y/G})$ is torsion free.
    
    (ii) This follows since $\pi_Y^*(H_1(\Gamma_{Y/G})) \otimes {\mathbf{Q}}=(H_1(\Gamma_Y)\otimes {\mathbf{Q}})^G$ and $f_{2,*}\circ f_1^*$ commutes with the action of $G$.
    
    (iii) Since $H_1(\Gamma_{Y})$ is torsion free, it suffices to show this after tensoring with ${\mathbf{Q}}$. By $(ii)$ both maps have images contained in $\pi_Y^*( H_1(\Gamma_{Y/G})\otimes {\mathbf{Q}})$ and so by $(i)$ it suffices to show equality after composing with $\pi_{Y,*}$. The statement follows since
    \begin{align*}     
   \pi_{Y,*} \circ f_{2,*} \circ f_1^* \circ \pi_Y^{*}&= 
    g_{2,*}\circ \pi_{X,*} \circ \pi_X^{*} \circ g_1^*=
     g_{2,*} \circ [\#G] \circ g_1^*\\
     & =    [\#G] \circ g_{2,*} \circ g_1^*
    =\pi_{Y,*} \circ \pi_Y^{*} \circ g_{2,*} \circ g_1^*.
    \end{align*}
    In the last part, we used that the actions of $G$ on both $X$ and $Y$ are faithful as this ensures that both $\pi_{X,*} \circ \pi_X^{*} $ and $\pi_{Y,*} \circ \pi_Y^{*}$ are multiplication by $\#G$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:computing_Tq}
    Let $\ell,p,N,M,W$ be as in \Cref{setup:al_quotient_hecke}, and $\pi:X_0(N) \to X_0(N)/W$ be the quotient map. Let $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ be a basis of $H_1(\mathcal{G}_W)$ and $\pi^*(e_1),\ldots,\pi^*(e_n)$ be the corresponding basis of $\pi^*(H_1(\mathcal{G}_W))  \subseteq H_1(\mathcal{G}_0(N))$. Then the matrices expressing the actions of $T_p$ on the basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ and on the basis $\pi^*(e_1),\ldots,\pi^*(e_n)$ are the same.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
\label{def:L_ell}
Let $N=\ell M$ be squarefree. We denote by $L_\ell=L_\ell(N)$ the number of \emph{long loops} of $\mathcal{G}_0(N)^*$, i.e.\ loops $e$ with $l(e)>1$.
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:L_ell_is_also_ODP_count}
 As $X_0(N)^*$ is semi-stable over ${\mathbf{Z}}_\ell$, by \Cref{def:reduction_graph} (with $r=1$), $L_\ell$ is also the number of ordinary double points of $(X_0(N)^*)_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell}$ of thickness $>1$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:atLeast_g_minus_Ll_heights}
Let $N$ be a squarefree integer, $p\nmid N$ a prime and $b \in X_0(N)^*({\mathbf{Q}})$ the unique cusp. Then there are at least $$g(X_0(N)^*) -1- \sum_{\ell \mid N} L_\ell(N)$$
linearly independent $p$-adic heights supported at $p$ using $b$ as a basepoint.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
As a shorthand, let $\NS$ denote the Néron--Severi group $\NS(J_0(N)^*)\otimes {\mathbf{Q}}$ and $\NS^{\tr=0}$ its subspace of trace-zero correspondences. The space of all $p$-adic heights with basepoint $b$ is parametrized by $\NS^{\tr=0}$. By \Cref{lem:hecke_is_End} the rank of the Néron--Severi group equals $g(X_0(N)^*)$.

Let $\ell \mid N$ be a prime, $Z \in \NS^{\tr=0}$ be a correspondence, and $\mathcal{G}_0(N)^*$ be the dual graph of $X_0(N)^*$ over ${\mathbf{F}}_\ell$. Let $F_Z$ be the endomorphism of $H_1(\mathcal{G}_0(N)^*)$ induced by $Z$. The dual graph $\mathcal{G}_0(N)^*$ of $X_0(N)^*$ is a flower graph by \Cref{cor:dual_graph_quotient}.  So by \Cref{lem:local_height_vanishes_long_edges} one has $h_\ell(X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell))=0$ as soon as $e^*F_Z (\pi(e))=0$ for every long edge $e$ of $\mathcal{G}_0(N)^*$. The lemma now follows since $e^*F_Z (\pi(e))$ depends linearly on $Z$, and hence the condition $h_\ell(X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell))=0$ is implied by $L_\ell(N)$ linear conditions on $Z \in \NS^{\tr=0}$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:clean_criterion}
Let $N$ be squarefree and $p\nmid N$ a prime. If $g(X_0(N)^*)>1+\sum_{\ell\mid N}L_\ell(N)$, then there is a $p$-adic height on $X_0(N)^*$ supported at $p$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:local_height_vanishes_long_edges}
Let $X$ be a stable curve over ${\mathbf{Q}}_\ell$ whose dual graph $\mathcal{G}$ is a flower graph. Call an edge $e\in E(\mathcal{G})$ \emph{long} if $l(e)>1$. Let $Z$ be a trace-zero correspondence on $X$, let $F$ be the endomorphism induced by $Z$ at $\ell$ (\Cref{def:corr_endomorphism}) and let $\mu_F$ be its measure (\Cref{def:corr_measure}). Assume that $\mu_F$ vanishes along every long edge, i.e.\ that
\[
    e^*F\left(\pi(e)\right)=0\qquad\text{for every long }e\in E(\mathcal{G}).
\]
Then $h_\ell(z)=0$ for every $z\in X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
First note that if $X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell) = \emptyset$ then there is nothing to prove. So we assume $X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell) \neq \emptyset$ and chose a basepoint $b \in X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$.
Let $e_1,\dots,e_r$ be the edges of $\mathcal{G}$, which are loops at its unique vertex $v_0$, and put $l_j\colonequals l(e_j)\in{\mathbf{Z}}_{\geqslant1}$. The minimal regular model subdivides $e_j$ into $l_j$ segments of length $1$, the $l_j-1$ interior vertices corresponding to the components of a chain of ${\mathbf{P}}^1$'s, by \cite[Corollary~10.3.25]{Liu2002}. Let $V$ be the set of vertices of this subdivision, that is, $v_0$ together with the interior vertices of the long loops; we have $\mathrm{red}\left(X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)\right)\subseteq V$.                              

Let $j_\mathcal{G}$ be as in \Cref{thm:BDMTV_localheight} and let $c_j\in{\mathbf{Q}}_p$ be the density of the edge part of $\mu_F$ along $e_j$. We claim that $j_\mathcal{G}$ is constant of value $j_\mathcal{G}(v_0)$ on $V$. Indeed, fix $j$ and identify $e_j$ with $[0,l_j]$; as $e_j$ is a loop at $v_0$, its source and its target are both $v_0$, so the two endpoint values are both equal to $j_\mathcal{G}(v_0)$. If $l_j=1$, then $e_j$ has no interior vertex and there is nothing to prove. If $l_j>1$, then $e_j$ is long, so $c_j=0$ by hypothesis, and the interior vertices of $e_j$ are rational curves; \Cref{lem:quadratic_along_edge} applies and gives $j_\mathcal{G}(x)=j_\mathcal{G}(v_0)$ for all $x\in e_j$. This proves the claim.

The basepoint $b$ lies in $X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$, so $\mathrm{red}(b)\in V$. Since $j_\mathcal{G}(\mathrm{red}(b))=0$ and $j_\mathcal{G}$ is constant on $V$ by the claim, $j_\mathcal{G}$ vanishes on $V$. Hence $j_\mathcal{G}\left(\mathrm{red}(z)\right)=0$ for every $z\in X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$. As $h_\ell$ is a constant multiple of $j_\mathcal{G}\circ\mathrm{red}$, the lemma follows.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:flower_heights}
For the flower graph $\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}_0(N)^*$ of \Cref{def:dual_graph_quotient} the boundary map $\partial\colon{\mathbf{Q}}\,E(\mathcal{G})\to{\mathbf{Q}}\,V(\mathcal{G})$ vanishes, so $\mathrm H_1(\mathcal{G},{\mathbf{Q}})={\mathbf{Q}}\,E(\mathcal{G})$ and $\pi=\mathrm{id}$. Writing $F_{jj}=e_j^*F(e_j)$ for the diagonal entry of $F$ in the basis of loops, the density of $\mu_F$ along $e_j$ is therefore $c_j=F_{jj}/l_j$, and \Cref{lem:quadratic_along_edge} with $a=b=0$ gives
\[
  j_\mathcal{G}|_{e_j}(x)=\frac{F_{jj}}{2\,l_j}\,x\,(x-l_j),\qquad x\in\{0,1,\dots,l_j\}.
\]
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
Let $X$ be as in \Cref{lem:local_height_vanishes_long_edges} and $b\in X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$ a basepoint such that $b_{{\mathbf{F}}_\ell}$ specialises to the central vertex $v_0$ of the flower graph.  Assume that all ordinary double points of $X_{{\mathbf{F}}_\ell}$ are split. 

If there is a long edge $e \in E(\mathcal{G})$ such that
\[
    e^*F\left(\pi(e)\right)\neq 0.
\]
Then there is an $z\in X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$ such that $h_\ell(z)\neq 0$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Identify $e$ with $[0,l]$, where $l\colonequals l(e)\geqslant 2$, and let $c\colonequals\tfrac1l\,e^*F\left(\pi(e)\right)\neq0$ be the density of the edge part of $\mu_F$ along $e$. Let $j_\mathcal{G}$ be as in \Cref{thm:BDMTV_localheight}. As $\mathrm{red}(b)=v_0$, the normalisation of $j_\mathcal{G}$ gives $j_\mathcal{G}(v_0)=0$. Since $e$ is a loop at $v_0$, both endpoint values of $j_\mathcal{G}$ on $e$ are $0$, and the interior vertices of $e$ correspond to rational curves, so \Cref{lem:quadratic_along_edge} gives
\[
  j_\mathcal{G}(x)=-\tfrac{c}{2}\,x\,(x-l)\qquad\text{for } x\in[0,l].
\]
In particular $j_\mathcal{G}(1)=\tfrac{c}{2}(l-1)\neq0$.

It remains to find $z\in X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$ that reduces to the vertex $w$ at $x=1$ on $e$. Let $\mathcal X'$ be the minimal regular model of $X$. Since the double point corresponding to $e$ is split, by \Cref{cor:regual_from_semistable_model} the component $C_w$ of $\mathcal X'_{{\mathbf{F}}_\ell}$ corresponding to $w$ is a projective line over ${\mathbf{F}}_\ell$ of multiplicity $1$, which meets the other components in two points. As $\#{\mathbf{P}}^1({\mathbf{F}}_\ell)=\ell+1\geqslant3$, there is a point $y\in C_w({\mathbf{F}}_\ell)$ lying on no other component. Then $\mathcal X'$ is smooth over ${\mathbf{Z}}_\ell$ at $y$, so by Hensel's lemma $y$ lifts to a point $z\in\mathcal X'({\mathbf{Z}}_\ell)=X({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$ with $\mathrm{red}(z)=w$. Hence $h_\ell(z)=\kappa\, j_\mathcal{G}(w)=\kappa\,\tfrac{c}{2}(l-1)\neq0$, as $\kappa\neq0$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:extra_automorphism}
 Let $\ell$ be a prime, $M$ be a squarefree integer coprime to $\ell$ and $N=M\ell$. The number of supersingular points $(E,G)=x \in X_0(N)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$ with $\#\Aut(E,G) > 2$ is at most $(1+c_\ell) 2^{\omega(N)}$ where
 $$ c_\ell \colonequals \begin{cases}
     0\text{ if } \ell>3\\
     1 \text{ if } \ell=3\\
     \frac 5 2 \text{ if } \ell=2.
 \end{cases}$$
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
By \Cref{prop:aut_classification} a supersingular point $x=(E,G)$ can have $\#\Aut(E,G)>2$ only if $\#\Aut(E)>2$, that is, only if $j(E)\equiv0$ or $1728\pmod \ell$. An automorphism $\gamma\in\Aut(E)$ of order $\ell\in\{3,4\}$ generates a subring ${\mathbf{Z}}[\gamma]\cong{\mathbf{Z}}[\zeta_\ell]$ of $\End(E)$, and $\gamma\in\Aut(E,G)$ if and only if $\gamma(G)=G$.

\emph{A counting bound.}
Fix such a $\gamma$ of order $\ell$ and let us bound the number of cyclic subgroups $G\subseteq E$ of order $M$ with $\gamma(G)=G$. For each prime $q\mid M$ we have $q\ne \ell$, so $E[q]\cong({\mathbf{Z}}/q{\mathbf{Z}})^2$ and $G_q\colonequals G \cap E[q]$ is a line in $E[q]$ with $\gamma(G_q)=G_q$; conversely $G=\bigoplus_{q\mid M}G_q$ is recovered from the family $(G_q)_{q\mid M}$. Now $\gamma$ acts ${\mathbf{F}}_q$-linearly on $E[q]$ with minimal polynomial $X^2+1$ (if $\ell=4$) or $X^2+X+1$ (if $\ell=3$); its eigenvalues are primitive $\ell$-th roots of unity, so $\gamma$ is \emph{not} a scalar on $E[q]$ (for $q=2$ note that $\gamma$ maps to an element of order $2$ resp.\ $3$ in $\Aut(E[2])=\GL_2({\mathbf{F}}_2)$, again non-scalar). A non-scalar element of $\GL_2({\mathbf{F}}_q)$ leaves at most two lines invariant, so there are at most two choices for $G_q$, and hence at most $2^{\omega(M)}$ subgroups $G$ with $\gamma(G)=G$.

A point $(E,G)$ satisfies $\#\Aut(E,G)>2$ if and only if $\Aut(E,G)$ contains an element of order $3$, $4$ or $6$; since the square of an order-$6$ element has order $3$ and fixes the same $G$, this happens precisely when $G$ is invariant under a generator of one of the cyclic subgroups of order $3$ or $4$ of $\Aut(E)$. Writing $s_\ell$ for the number of subgroups of order $\ell$ of $\Aut(E)$, the number of extra-automorphism points supported on a fixed curve $E$ is therefore at most $(s_3+s_4)\,2^{\omega(M)}$.

\emph{Case $\ell>3$.} Here $\#\Aut(E)>2$ forces $j(E)=1728$ (so $\Aut(E)\cong C_4$, $s_3=0$, $s_4=1$) or $j(E)=0$ (so $\Aut(E)\cong C_6$, $s_3=1$, $s_4=0$), and these are two distinct curves. Summing, the number of extra-automorphism points is at most $(1+1)\,2^{\omega(M)}=2^{\omega(N)}$, which is the claim with $c_\ell =0$.

\emph{Case $\ell\in\{2,3\}$.} Then $0\equiv1728\pmod \ell$ and there is a unique supersingular curve $E_0$ up to isomorphism \cite[Theorem~V.4.1]{Silverman1}. If $\ell=2$ this curve has $\Aut(E_0)\cong\SL_2({\mathbf{F}}_3)$ and $\Aut(E_0)\cong {\mathbf{Z}}/3{\mathbf{Z}} \rtimes {\mathbf{Z}}/4{\mathbf{Z}}$ if $\ell=3$ (\Cref{prop:aut_classification}). In $\SL_2({\mathbf{F}}_3)$ the normal Sylow $2$-subgroup $Q_8$ contains all three subgroups of order $4$, so $s_4=3$, and there are $s_3=4$ Sylow $3$-subgroups.  In ${\mathbf{Z}}/3{\mathbf{Z}} \rtimes {\mathbf{Z}}/4{\mathbf{Z}}$ one has $s_4=3$ and a unique (normal) $s_3=1$. Hence the number of extra-automorphism points is at most $(3+4)\,2^{\omega(M)}=\tfrac72\,2^{\omega(N)}$ when $\ell=2$, and at most $(3+1)\,2^{\omega(M)}=2\cdot2^{\omega(N)}$ when $\ell=3$. This proves one can take $c_2=\frac 5 2$ and $c_3 = 1$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
\label{def:SS_fixed_points}
    Let $\ell$ be a prime, $M$ be a squarefree integer coprime to $\ell$ and $d \mid \ell M$. Let $d$ be larger than $1$. Denote $N=\ell M$. Then $\nu_{\ell}(N,d)$ is defined to be the number of fixed points of $w_d$ in supersingular locus of $X_0(N)(\overline {\mathbf{F}}_\ell)$.
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:Bpnw}
    For every prime \(\ell  \mid N\) the number of ordinary double points in $(X_0(N)/W)_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell}$ of thickness $>1$ is at most 
    \begin{align*}
       B(\ell,N,W) \colonequals  \frac 2 {\#W} \left((1+c_\ell)2^{\omega(N)} + \sum_{1<d \mid M, w_d\in W}\nu_{\ell}(N,d)\right)
    \end{align*} 
    where $c_\ell$ is as in Proposition \ref{prop:extra_automorphism}. In particular, we have $L_\ell(N) \leqslant B(\ell,N, W_N)$, where $L_\ell(N)$ is as in \Cref{def:L_ell}.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
According to \Cref{thm:semi-stable_star} the ordinary double points of thickness $>1$ come from supersingular points in $(E,G) = x \in X_0(N)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$ such that either $\# \Aut(E,G)>2$ or $w_d x=x$ for some $w_d \in W$ with $d \mid M$ and $d > 1$. 

First we look at the contribution coming from those points where $\# \Aut(E,G) > 2$. By \Cref{prop:extra_automorphism} there are at most $(1+c_\ell)2^{\omega(N)}$ such supersingular points $(E,G)$, so they account for at most $(1+c_\ell)2^{\omega(N)}/\#W$ points of $(X_0(N)/W)_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell}$; this contributes at most $2(1+c_\ell)2^{\omega(N)}/\#W$ to the bound $B(\ell,N,W)$. (For $\ell>3$ this recovers the count $2\cdot2^{\omega(N)}/\#W$, since then $c_\ell =0$ and $E$ is one of the two curves with $j\equiv0,1728$, of automorphism type ${\mathbf{Z}}/4{\mathbf{Z}}$ or ${\mathbf{Z}}/6{\mathbf{Z}}$; for $\ell\in\{2,3\}$ the extra factor $c_\ell $ accounts for the larger automorphism group of the supersingular curve.)

Now for the contribution to those points that are fixed by some $w_d$ with $1 < d \mid M$. To this end, let $S \subseteq X_0(N)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$ be the subset of supersingular points that are fixed by at least one Atkin--Lehner operator $w_d\in W$ with $d\mid M$, $d>1$. As $W$ is abelian, this set is stable under the action of $W$. There will be $\#(S/W)$ points of thickness $>1$ coming from this set. We bound the cardinality of $\#(S/W)$ using Burnside's Lemma. 
\begin{align}
    \#(S/W) = \frac 1 {\#W}\left(\#S+ \sum_{1<d \mid M, w_d\in W}\nu_{\ell}(N,d)\right)
\end{align}
The first part of the theorem follows since
\[
    \#S \leqslant \sum_{1<d \mid M, w_d\in W}\nu_{\ell}(N,d). \qedhere
\]
The fact that $L_\ell(N) \leqslant B(\ell,N,W_N)$ follows from \Cref{rem:L_ell_is_also_ODP_count}.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:hecke_is_End}
Let $N$ be a squarefree integer, and let $\mathbb T\subseteq \End \, J_0(N)^*$ be the Hecke algebra generated by the Hecke operators $T_p$ with $p\nmid N$. Then $\mathbb T \otimes {\mathbf{Q}} = \End \, J_0(N)^* \, \otimes {\mathbf{Q}} \cong \NS(J_0(N)^*) \otimes {\mathbf{Q}}$, and all three have dimension $g\colonequals g(X_0(N)^*)$ over ${\mathbf{Q}}$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Clearly $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}\subseteq\End \, J_0(N)^*\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$. By Atkin--Lehner theory \cite{AtkinLehner1970}, the space $S_2(\Gamma_0(N))^{W_N}\cong H^0(X_0(N)^*,\Omega^1)$, of dimension $g$, has a basis of eigenforms for $\mathbb T$ with pairwise distinct systems of eigenvalues. Indeed, taking $W_N$-invariants causes all old forms to occur with multiplicity 1. Hence, the image of $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{C}}$ seen as acting on modular forms contains the $g$ projections onto these eigenlines, so $\dim_{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}\geqslant g$. On the other hand, since $N$ is squarefree, $\End \, J_0(N)^*\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}\cong\prod_i K_i$ is a product of totally real number fields \cite[\S2, before Corollary~2.6]{BakerHasegawa}. Accordingly, $J_0(N)^*$ is isogenous to a product of abelian varieties $J_i$ with $\End \, J_i\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}\cong K_i$, and $[K_i:{\mathbf{Q}}]\leqslant\dim J_i$ since $K_i$ is totally real \cite[\S21]{Mumford}. Hence $\dim_{\mathbf{Q}} \End \, J_0(N)^*\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}\leqslant g$, and therefore $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}=\End \, J_0(N)^*\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$.

By \cite[Proposition 17.2]{MilneAbelianVarieties}, $\NS(J_0(N)^*)\otimes {\mathbf{Q}}$ is isomorphic to the subspace of $\End \, J_0(N)^* \otimes {\mathbf{Q}}$ fixed by the Rosati involution. We will denote the Rosati involution by $\dagger$. As $\End \, J_0(N)^* \otimes {\mathbf{Q}}$ is a product of number fields, it is commutative, and hence the Rosati involution is an algebra morphism.  Positivity rules out swapping two factors, since for an idempotent $e$ of $K_i$ with $e^\dagger\in K_j$, $j\neq i$, we get $e\,e^\dagger=0$. Furthermore, a positive involution of a totally real field is trivial. So $\dagger$ is the identity and hence $\End \, J_0(N)^* \, \otimes {\mathbf{Q}} \cong \NS(J_0(N)^*) \otimes {\mathbf{Q}}$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- notation-1: body_md -->
\label{not:brandt_orbits}
Let $\ell\mid N$ be a prime, $M\colonequals N/\ell$, let $\mathcal{O}$ be an Eichler order of level $M$ in $B_{\ell,\infty}$, and let $I_1,\ldots,I_h$ be representatives of $\operatorname{Cls}\mathcal{O}$. An ideal class $I_k$ corresponds to a supersingular point $x_k\in X_0(N)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$ by Deuring's Correspondence (\Cref{thm:Deuring}). And by Deligne--Rapoport's description of the special fiber of $X_0(N)_{{\mathbf{F}}_\ell}$  (\Cref{thm:semi-stable_X0}~(ii)) the point $x_k\in X_0(N)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$ corresponds to an edge $e_k$ of $\mathcal{G}_0(N)$, which we orient from $v_0$ to $v_1$. Via $e_k\mapsto$ $k$-th standard basis vector we identify ${\mathbf{Q}}\,E(\mathcal{G}_0(N))$ with ${\mathbf{Q}}^h$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item The group $W_N$ acts on $\{1,\ldots,h\}$ via $w(x_k)=x_{w(k)}$. For $k\in\{1,\ldots,h\}$ we write $W_{x_k}\subseteq W_N$ for the stabiliser of $x_k$.
    \item Let $\varepsilon_\ell\colon W_N\to\{\pm1\}$ be the character with $\varepsilon_\ell(w_d)=-1$ if $\ell\mid d$ and $\varepsilon_\ell(w_d)=1$ otherwise.
    \item Let $R_\ell$ be the set of $W_N$-orbits $O\subseteq\{1,\ldots,h\}$ such that $\varepsilon_\ell$ is trivial on $W_{x_k}$ for one, equivalently all, $k\in O$. For $O\in R_\ell$ we fix $k_O\in O$ and put $l_O\colonequals\#W_{x_{k_O}}\cdot\tfrac12\#O_L(I_{k_O})^\times$ and
    \[
      \tilde e_O\colonequals\sum_{wW_{x_{k_O}}\in W_N/W_{x_{k_O}}}\varepsilon_\ell(w)\,e_{w(k_O)}\in{\mathbf{Q}}^h,
    \]
    which is well defined as $\varepsilon_\ell$ is trivial on $W_{x_{k_O}}$.
    \item Let $R_\ell^{\mathrm{long}}\colonequals\{O\in R_\ell : l_O>1\}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end notation-1 -->
<!-- algorithm-1: body_md -->
\label{alg:clean_correspondences}
\textbf{Input:} a squarefree integer $N$ and a prime $p\nmid N$ such that $T_p$ generates $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$.
 
\textbf{Output:} polynomials $f_1,\ldots,f_n\in{\mathbf{Q}}[x]$ as in \Cref{prop:correspondence_algorithm}.
 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{Step \arabic*.}, ref=\arabic*, leftmargin=*]
    \item\label{step:Tp_on_S} \emph{(The trace condition.)} Compute the matrix of $T_p$ acting on $S$ using modular symbols \cite[Chapter~8]{SteinBook}, and compute $\tau_i\colonequals\operatorname{tr}(T_p^i)$ for $0\leqslant i\leqslant g-1$.
    \item\label{step:brandt} \emph{(The local conditions.)} For every prime $\ell\mid N$:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), ref=\arabic{enumi}(\alph*)]
        \item Compute the action of the Hecke operator $T_p$ on the Brandt module ${\mathbf{Q}}[\operatorname{Cls}\mathcal{O}]={\mathbf{Q}}^h$ using the ideas of \cite{KohelHecke};
        \item Similarly compute the action of $W_N$ on $\{1,\ldots,h\}$ using the ideas of \cite{KohelHecke}.
        \item Compute the stabilisers $W_{x_k}$, the unit groups $\#O_L(I_k)^\times$, the sets $R_\ell\supseteq R_\ell^{\mathrm{long}}$ and the vectors $\tilde e_O$ for $O\in R_\ell$;
        \item Compute the matrix $A_\ell$ of $B_\ell(p)$ acting on the span of the $\tilde e_O$, $O\in R_\ell$, with respect to the basis $(\tilde e_O)_{O\in R_\ell}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item\label{step:linalg} \emph{(Linear algebra.)} Compute a basis $c^{(1)},\ldots,c^{(n)}$ of the space of vectors $c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{g-1})\in{\mathbf{Q}}^g$ satisfying
    \[
      \sum_{i=0}^{g-1} c_i\,\tau_i=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{i=0}^{g-1} c_i\,(A_\ell^i)_{O,O}=0\quad\text{for all }\ell\mid N\text{ and }O\in R_\ell^{\mathrm{long}},
    \]
    and output $f_j\colonequals\sum_{i=0}^{g-1}c_i^{(j)}x^i$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end algorithm-1 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
We show that the output of \Cref{alg:clean_correspondences} has the required properties. By \Cref{lem:hecke_is_End}, $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$ has dimension $g$. As it is generated by $T_p$, the elements $1,T_p,\ldots,T_p^{g-1}$ form a basis of $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$. The linear system in Step~\ref{step:linalg} consists of $1+\sum_{\ell\mid N}\#R_\ell^{\mathrm{long}}$ equations in $g$ unknowns. We show below that $\#R_\ell^{\mathrm{long}}=L_\ell(N)$, so $n\geqslant g-1-\sum_{\ell\mid N}L_\ell(N)$. If $g\leqslant1$ then $n=0$, as $\tau_0=g$, and there is nothing else to prove. So we assume $g\geqslant2$.
 
\emph{Trace zero and linear independence.} Let $t\in\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$. Then $\mathrm H^1_{\dR}(X_0(N)^*_{\mathbf{C}})$ is the direct sum of $H^0(X_0(N)^*_{\mathbf{C}},\Omega^1)\cong S\otimes{\mathbf{C}}$ and its complex conjugate, and $t$ acts on the latter by the complex conjugate of its action on the former. As $\operatorname{tr}(t)\in{\mathbf{Q}}$, the trace of $t$ on $\mathrm H^1_{\dR}$ equals $2\operatorname{tr}(t)$, so $t$ has trace zero if and only if $\operatorname{tr}(t)=0$. For $f=\sum_ic_ix^i$ we have $\operatorname{tr}(f(T_p))=\sum_ic_i\tau_i$, so by the first equation in Step~\ref{step:linalg} each $f_j(T_p)$ has trace zero. As the vectors $c^{(j)}$ are linearly independent, so are $f_1(T_p),\ldots,f_n(T_p)$. By \Cref{lem:hecke_is_End} these are elements of $\End\,J_0(N)^*\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}\cong\NS(J_0(N)^*)\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$, so they give rise to linearly independent $p$-adic heights.
 
\emph{Supported at $p$.} Since $X_0(N)^*$ has good reduction at all primes not dividing $N$, it suffices to show that for every $\ell\mid N$ and every $f=f_j$, the local height $h_\ell$ with respect to $t\colonequals f(T_p)$ vanishes on $X_0(N)^*({\mathbf{Q}}_\ell)$. Fix $\ell$. As $w_\ell\in W_N$, the curve $X_0(N)^*$ is stable over ${\mathbf{Z}}_\ell$ with dual graph the flower graph $\mathcal{G}\colonequals\mathcal{G}_0(N)^*$ by \Cref{thm:semi-stable_star}~(iv) and \Cref{cor:dual_graph_quotient}. Every endomorphism of $J_0(N)^*$ preserves the filtration on $V_p(X_0(N)^*)$, so the construction of \Cref{def:corr_endomorphism} gives a ring homomorphism $\End\,J_0(N)^*\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}\to\End\,\mathrm H_1(\mathcal{G},{\mathbf{Q}})$, $s\mapsto F_s$. In particular $F_t=f(F_{T_p})$. So by \Cref{lem:local_height_vanishes_long_edges} and \Cref{rem:flower_heights}, it suffices to show that the diagonal entry of $f(F_{T_p})$ at every long loop of $\mathcal{G}$ vanishes, with respect to the basis of $\mathrm H_1(\mathcal{G},{\mathbf{Q}})={\mathbf{Q}}\,E(\mathcal{G})$ given by the loops.
 
By \Cref{def:dual_graph_quotient}, the loops of $\mathcal{G}$ correspond to the $W_N$-orbits of supersingular points $x\in X_0(N)({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$ that are not fixed by any $w_{\ell d}$, and the loop corresponding to the orbit of $x=(E,G)$ has length $\#W_x\cdot\tfrac12\#\Aut(E,G)$. As the $w_{\ell d}$ are exactly the elements of $W_N$ on which $\varepsilon_\ell$ is $-1$, and $\#\Aut(E,G)=\#O_L(I_k)^\times$ for $x=x_k$ by \Cref{thm:Deuring}, the loops of $\mathcal{G}$ correspond to the orbits $O\in R_\ell$. The loop $e_O$ corresponding to $O$ has length $l_O$, so the long loops correspond to the $O\in R_\ell^{\mathrm{long}}$; in particular $\#R_\ell^{\mathrm{long}}=L_\ell(N)$.
 
Let $\pi\colon X_0(N)\to X_0(N)^*$ be the quotient map. By \Cref{thm:semi-stable_X0}~(ii), $w_d$ swaps $v_0$ and $v_1$ if and only if $\ell\mid d$, so $w\in W_N$ maps $e_k$ to $\varepsilon_\ell(w)\,e_{w(k)}$. The element $\pi^*(e_O)$ is $W_N$-invariant and non-zero (\Cref{lem:quotient-correspondence}), and it is supported on the edges $e_k$ lying over $e_O$, i.e.\ on those with $k\in O$. For such a vector the coefficient at $e_{w(k_O)}$ is $\varepsilon_\ell(w)$ times the coefficient at $e_{k_O}$. Hence $\pi^*(e_O)=\lambda_O\tilde e_O$ for some $\lambda_O\in{\mathbf{Q}}^\times$. In particular, the span of the $\tilde e_O$ is $\pi^*(\mathrm H_1(\mathcal{G},{\mathbf{Q}}))$, which is stable under $T_p$ by \Cref{lem:quotient-correspondence}~(ii), so $A_\ell$ in Step~\ref{step:brandt}(d) is well defined. The action of $T_p$ on $\mathrm H_1(\mathcal{G}_0(N),{\mathbf{Q}})\subseteq{\mathbf{Q}}^h$ is given by the Brandt matrix $B_\ell(p)$ \cite[p.~445]{Ribet1990}, \cite[Theorem~4.3]{KohelHecke}. By \Cref{cor:computing_Tq}, the matrix of $F_{T_p}$ with respect to the basis $(e_O)_{O\in R_\ell}$ is therefore $D^{-1}A_\ell D$, where $D$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $\lambda_O$. So $f(F_{T_p})$ corresponds to $D^{-1}f(A_\ell)D$, whose diagonal entry at $e_O$ is $\sum_ic_i(A_\ell^i)_{O,O}$. For $O\in R_\ell^{\mathrm{long}}$ this vanishes by the second set of equations in Step~\ref{step:linalg}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:Tp_generator}
By the proof of \Cref{lem:hecke_is_End}, $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$ is a product of number fields. Hence $T_p$ generates $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$ if and only if the characteristic polynomial of $T_p$ acting on $S$ is squarefree, which is easy to check. This condition does not hold for every $p$. For example, let $N=37\cdot43$. The elliptic curves \textnormal{\href{https://www.lmfdb.org/EllipticCurve/Q/37.a1/}{\texttt{37.a1}}} and \textnormal{\href{https://www.lmfdb.org/EllipticCurve/Q/43.a1/}{\texttt{43.a1}}} have root number $-1$, so the Atkin--Lehner eigenvalues of their newforms are $+1$. Each of them therefore contributes a line to $S$, on which $T_2$ acts by $a_2=-2$. So $T_2$ does not generate $\mathbb T\otimes{\mathbf{Q}}$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label[theorem]{prop:2to1}
    Let $\ell,M,N,d$ be as in \Cref{def:SS_fixed_points}.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item If $d>2$, then $\nu_{\ell}(N,d)$ is equal to half the number of \(\mathcal{O}^\times\)-conjugacy classes of embeddings of ${\mathbf{Z}}[\sqrt{-d}]$ into an Eichler order of level $M$ in $B_{\ell,\infty}$, where $\mathcal{O}$ ranges over the corresponding Eichler orders of level $M$ in $B_{\ell,\infty}$.

         \item If $d=2$, then $\nu_{\ell}(N,2)$ is equal to half the total number of \(\mathcal{O}^\times\)-conjugacy classes of embeddings in the disjoint union of the two embedding problems
        ${\mathbf{Z}}[\sqrt{-2}]\hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}$ and ${\mathbf{Z}}[\sqrt{-1}]\hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}$,
        where $\mathcal{O}$ ranges over the corresponding Eichler orders of level $M$ in $B_{\ell,\infty}$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The embeddings in the above theorem do not need to be optimal.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:wdInduceEnd}
Let $\ell,M,N,d$ be as in \Cref{def:SS_fixed_points} and $(E,G) \in X_0(N)_{{\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell }$ be a supersingular point. Then 
$(E,G)$ is a fixed point of $w_d$ if and only if there is an $h \in \End(E,G)$ and a $\varphi \in \Aut(E)$ such that
\[
h^2 = \varphi\circ[d].
\]
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
We consider a point $x\in X_0(N)$ as a pair of $(E, G)$ where $G$ is a cyclic subgroup of size $N$. For $d\mid N$, we can decompose $G = G[d] \oplus G[N/d]$ and then write the action of Atkin--Lehner involution as $w_d(E,G)=w_d(E,G[d],G[N/d])=(E/G[d],\; E[d]/G[d],\; G/G[d])$. Recall that $N=\ell M$ is squarefree, so $\gcd(d,N/d)=1$ and the direct-sum decomposition $G=G[d]\oplus G[N/d]$ is legitimate.

Hence $w_d(E,G)\sim (E,G)$ is equivalent to \[ (E/G[d], E[d]/G[d], G/G[d]) \sim (E, G[d], G[N/d]),\]
and this is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uivalentCondOng} \text{there exists a }\, g:E/G[d] \longrightarrow E
\text{ such that } 
\begin{cases}
g\big(E[d]/G[d]\big)=G[d],\\[2pt]
g\big(G/G[d]\big)=G[N/d].
\end{cases}
\end{equation}

Now assume $w_d(E,G)\sim (E,G)$. Taking both of these equivalent descriptions, we get a map
\[
h\colon E \longrightarrow E/G[d] \overset{g}{\longrightarrow} E,
\]
where \(\ker h=G[d]\) is of size \(d\).
Since \(h\big(E[d]\big)=G[d]\), we have
\[
\ker(h^2)=E[d] = \ker [d],
\]
                                                                    
                         
Since multiplication by $[d]$ and $h^2$ have the same kernel, we get \(h^2=\varphi\circ[d]\) for some
\(\varphi\in \Aut(E)\).

To prove the other direction, assume that there is an $h\in\End(E,G)$ such that $\ker(h^2) = \ker [d]$. Since $d^2 = \deg[d] = \deg(h^2)=(\deg h)^2$, it follows that $\ker h$ is of size $d$.

For a prime $q\mid d$, since $h(G[q]) \subseteq G[q]$ (note that we assume $h(G) \subseteq G$ since $h \in \End(E,G)$), it follows that $h(G[q])$ is either $0$ (a trivial group) or $h(G[q])=G[q]$. If $h(G[q]) = G[q]$, then $0 = [d](G[q]) = h^2(G[q])=h(G[q])$ (here we use $q \mid d$), which is a contradiction. Hence $h(G[q])=0$ for all primes $q\mid d$, and $h(G[d])=0$ consequently. This means our $h$ factors through projection $\pi\colon E \rightarrow E/G[d]$, so $h=g \circ \pi$. It is straightforward to check the conditions in $\eqref{eq:uivalentCondOng}$ to hold for $g$, which is equivalent to $(E, G)$ being a fixed point of $w_d$; there are conditions: (a) $g(E[d]/G[d])=G[d]$ and (b) $g(G/G[d])=G[N/d]$. For (a): $g(E[d]/G[d])=h(E[d])$, and $\ker(h^2)=E[d]$ forces $h(E[d])\subseteq\ker h=G[d]$; since $|h(E[d])|=|E[d]|/|G[d]|=d^2/d=d=|G[d]|$, equality holds. For (b): $h(G[d])=0$, so $h(G)=h(G[N/d])$, which is injective of order $N/d$ and contained in $G$; as $G$ is cyclic it has a unique subgroup of that order, namely $G[N/d]$, so $g(G/G[d])=h(G)=G[N/d]$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:differByUnit}
Let $x=(E, G)$ be a $w_d$-fixed point of $X_0(N)_{\overline{{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell }$ and put $\mathcal{O}=\End(E, G)$. Suppose that $a, b\in \mathcal{O}$ are obtained from two choices of an isomorphism $w_d(x) \cong x$. Then there is a unique $u \in \mathcal{O}^\times$ such that $b=ua$. Conversely, if $a$ comes from one such choice and $u\in \mathcal{O}^\times$, then $ua$ comes from another such choice.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
In other words, the set of isomorphisms $w_d(x)\cong x$ is a torsor under $\mathcal{O}^\times$ (acting by post-composition), and the map sending such an isomorphism to its endomorphism $h$ is $\mathcal{O}^\times$-equivariant and injective; hence the resulting $h$ form a single free $\mathcal{O}^\times$-orbit.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
By proof of \cref{lem:wdInduceEnd}, both $a$ and $b$ factor through the same quotient $\pi : E \to E/G[d]$, and both have kernel $G[d]$. We can write $a = g_a \circ \pi$, $b=g_b \circ \pi$, where $g_a, g_b\colon E/G[d] \to E$ are isomorphisms satisfying the conditions \eqref{eq:uivalentCondOng} defining an isomorphism $w_d(x)\cong x$. Hence $u=g_b \circ g_a^{-1} \in \Aut(E,G)$, i.e.~$u\in \mathcal{O}^\times$, and $b=ua$. Since $a$ is an isogeny, uniqueness follows. Conversely, composing an isomorphism $w_d(x)\cong x$ with an element \( u \in \mathcal{O}^\times=\Aut(E, G)\) gives another such isomorphism (as \(u\) preserves both \(G[d]\) and \( G[n/d]\)).
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:traces}
Let $\ell, M, N, d$ be as in \cref{def:SS_fixed_points}, and let $x=(E,G)$ be a supersingular $w_d$-fixed point of $X_0(N)_{\overline{{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell }$ and $\mathcal{O}=\End(E,G)$. After choosing an isomorphism $w_d(x)\cong x$, let $h\in \mathcal{O}$ be the endomorphism given by \cref{lem:wdInduceEnd}. Then $\nrd(h)=d$. If $T=\trd(h)$, then $d\mid T$ and $T^2 < 4d$. Consequently:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $d > 3$, then $T=0$ and $h^2=-[d]$.
    \item If $d=3$, then $T\in\{ 0, \pm 3\}$. In all cases there is an element $t\in \mathcal{O}$ such that $t^2=-[3]$.
    \item If $d=2$, then $T\in\{0, \pm 2\}$. More precisely, if $T=0$, then $h^2=-[2]$; if $T=2$, then $(h-1)^2=-1$; and if $T=-2$, then $(h+1)^2=-1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
First we prove \emph{(i)} \fbox{\(d>3\)}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:wdInduceEnd}, after choosing
an isomorphism \(w_d(x)\cong x\), we obtain an element \(h\in \mathcal{O}\) and an
automorphism \(\varphi\in\Aut(E)\) such that \(h^2=\varphi\circ[d]\). Since the dual
$\hat{}$ induces the standard involution, \(\operatorname{nrd}(h)=\deg h=d\).
Write \(T=\trd(h)\). Then   
\(h^2-Th+d=0\), and therefore \(\varphi=h^2/d=(T/d)h-1\). Taking reduced traces gives \(\trd(\varphi)=T^2/d-2\). Since \(\varphi\) is an element of an order \(\End(E)\), we get \( \trd(\varphi)\in{\mathbf{Z}} \). As \(d\) is squarefree,
this implies \(d\mid T\). Since \(B_{\ell,\infty}\otimes_{{\mathbf{Q}}}{\mathbf{R}} \cong \bH\), a
non-scalar element of reduced norm \(d\) and reduced trace \(T\) satisfies
\(T^2<4d\). Indeed, writing \(h=a+v\), with \(a\in{\mathbf{R}}\) and \(v\) purely
quaternionic, one has \(T=2a\) and \(d=a^2+\|v\|^2\), and the inequality is
strict unless \(v=0\). In our situation \(h\) cannot be scalar, because then
its reduced norm would be a rational square, but \(\operatorname{nrd}(h)=d\)
and \(d>1\) is squarefree. Hence \(d\mid T\) and
\(T^2<4d\).

If \(d>3\), these conditions force \(T=0\) and thus \(h^2=-[d]\). (Hence $\varphi = h^2/d = [-1]$.)
If $(ii)$ \fbox{$d=3$}, then $T\in\{0, \pm 3\}$. If $T=0$, again $h^2=-[3]$. If $T=3$, then $h^2-3h+3=0$, so $(2h-3)^2=-3$. If $T=-3$, then $h^2+3h+3=0$ and $(2h+3)^2=-3$. In all cases there is $t\in \mathcal{O}$ such that $t^2=-[3]$.

The case $(iii)$ \fbox{$d=2$} is analogous. Now $T\in \{0, \pm 2\}$. If $T=0$, then $h^2=-[2]$. If $T=2$, then $h^2-2h+2=0$, so $(h-1)^2=-1$. If $T=-2$, then $h^2+2h+2=0$, so $(h+1)^2=-1$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
We note here that, for \( d=3 \), despite getting \(t\in \End(E, G)\) only after potentially modifying \( h\), since \( t^2 = -1 \circ [3]\), the converse direction of \cref{lem:wdInduceEnd} applies. This means that, for another embedding of \( \sqrt{-d}\) into \( \End(E, G) \), realized by \( s\in \End(E, G)\), by \cref{lem:differByUnit}, we can conclude \( s=ut\) for some unit \( u\).
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
We will use the following terminology. Let \(x=(E,G)\) be a \(w_d\)-fixed supersingular point, and put \(\mathcal{O}=\End(E,G)\). An \(\mathcal{O}^\times\)-conjugacy class in the relevant embedding problem is said to lie above \(x\) if it has a representative whose image is obtained from some choice of an isomorphism \(w_d(x)\cong x\), as follows.

Let \( h \in \mathcal{O} \) be the element obtained by \cref{lem:wdInduceEnd} from this choice. If \( d > 3\), then by \cref{lem:traces}\((i)\) we have \(h^2  = -d\), and the embedding \( {\mathbf{Z}}[\sqrt{-d}] \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}\) is sending \( \sqrt{-d} \mapsto h\). If \( d=3\), then by \cref{lem:traces}\((ii)\) we replace \( h\) by \( t = h\) if \( \trd(h)=0\), by \( t=2h-3\) if \( \trd(h)=3\), and by \( t = 2h+3 \) if \( \trd(h)=-3\). In each case, \(t^2 = -3\), and the embedding \( {\mathbf{Z}}[\sqrt{-3}] \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}\) is sending \( \sqrt{-3} \mapsto t\).

Similarly, if \( d=2 \),  we have two cases. If \(\trd(h)=0\), then \( \sqrt{-2} \mapsto h\),  while if \( \trd(h) = \pm 2\), then \( t=h\mp 1\), and \( \sqrt{-1} \mapsto t\).

An embedding in the relevant embedding problem is said to \emph{lie above} \( x\) if it can be obtained from \( x\), using this construction. A conjugacy class of embeddings is said to \emph{lie above} \(x\) if it contains an embedding lying above \( x\).

Note that, for \( d > 2\), we always get an embedding of \(\sqrt{-d}\), while for \(d=2\), this construction leads to embeddings of either \(\sqrt{-2}\) or \( \sqrt{-1}\).
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:unit_groups_cases}
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over $\overline{{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell $, and cyclic $G \subseteq E(\overline{{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell )$ of order $M$ with $\ell\nmid M$. Assume that either $\ell>3$ or that $M$ is divisible by a prime $q>3$, then $\Aut(E,G)$ is cyclic of order $2,4$ or $6$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Note that $-1 \in \Aut(E,G)$, so that the case $\ell>3$ as well as $j\not\equiv 0 \mod \ell$ with $\ell=2,3$ immediately follows from Proposition \ref{prop:aut_classification}.
So now the case where we have $q \mid M$ with $q$ a prime $>3$. Additionally from now on $\ell=2$ or $3$, $j=0$ and $\Aut(E)$ is either $\SL_2({\mathbf{F}}_3)$ if $\ell=2$ or ${\mathbf{Z}}/3{\mathbf{Z}} \rtimes {\mathbf{Z}}/4{\mathbf{Z}}$ if $\ell=3$. Note that $\Aut(E,G) \subseteq \Aut(E,G[q])$, so it suffices to prove the statement in the case $G=G[q]$ and $M=q$.  

We claim that $\Aut(E)$ acts faithfully on $E[q]({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell)$. Indeed, let $V_q(E) \colonequals \varprojlim_n E[q^n]({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell ) \cong {\mathbf{Z}}_q^2$ be the $q$-adic Tate module, then it is well known that \( \Aut(E) \) acts faithfully on $V_q(E)$. 
However, the reduction mod $q$ map $\GL_2({\mathbf{Z}}_q) \to \GL_2({\mathbf{F}}_q)$ is injective when restricted to elements of finite order coprime to $q$. So by Proposition \ref{prop:aut_classification} we get an injection $\Aut(E) \to \Aut(E[q]({\overline{\mathbf{F}}}_\ell ))$ and the claim follows.

Now as $\Aut(E)$ respects the Weil pairing, after a choice of basis of the $q$ torsion, we get that  $\Aut(E) \subseteq \SL_2({\mathbf{F}}_q)$. Since $\Aut(E,G)$ fixes $G$ we can choose a basis such that
\[
 \Aut(E,G) \subseteq U \colonequals \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & a^{-1} \end{pmatrix} : a \in {\mathbf{F}}_q^{\times},\; b \in {\mathbf{F}}_q \right\} \subseteq \mathrm{SL}_2({\mathbf{F}}_q).
\]
Note that $T \colonequals \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ generates a normal subgroup of order $q$ in $U$. Since $\Aut(E,G)$ has no elements of order $q$ we get an injection  $\Aut(E,G) \hookrightarrow U/\langle T \rangle \cong {\mathbf{F}}_q^\times$. This shows that $\Aut(E,G)$ is cyclic. And the proposition follows since ${\mathbf{Z}}/2{\mathbf{Z}}, {\mathbf{Z}}/4{\mathbf{Z}}$ and ${\mathbf{Z}}/6{\mathbf{Z}}$ are the only cyclic subgroups of $\Aut \, E$ containing $[-1]$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{lem:cyclic_two_classes}
Let \(\mathcal{O}\) be an order in a quaternion algebra over \({\mathbf{Q}}\), and assume \( \mathcal{O}^\times \cong C_2, C_4, C_6\). Let \( t\in \mathcal{O}\) satisfy \( t^2\in {\mathbf{Q}}^\times\), and put \( A = \{ u \in \mathcal{O}^\times: (ut)^2=t^2 \}\).

Then the elements \(ut\), with \( u \in A\), split into exactly two \( \mathcal{O}^\times \)-conjugacy classes.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
For \(u\in \mathcal{O}^\times\), the condition \((ut)^2=t^2\) is equivalent to
\(tut^{-1}=u^{-1}\) (note: \(t^{-1}\) exists in \(B^\times_{\ell,\infty}\)). Indeed, from \(utut=t^2\), left-multiplying by \(u^{-1}\)
gives \(tut=u^{-1}t^2\), hence \(tu=u^{-1}t\) and \(tut^{-1}=u^{-1}\). Thus \(A\) is a subgroup of \( \mathcal{O}^\times\) of the cyclic group \(\mathcal{O}^\times\). Since \( \{\pm 1\}\subseteq A \), either \( A=\{\pm1\} \)  or \( A = \mathcal{O}^\times\).

If \( A=\mathcal{O}^\times \), then for \( u,v\in \mathcal{O}^\times \), the condition for \( v^{-1} \) gives \(tv^{-1}=vt\), so
\(v(ut)v^{-1}=vu(tv^{-1})=vu(vt)=v^2ut\), since \(\mathcal{O}^\times\) is abelian. Thus
conjugating \(ut\) by \(v\) corresponds to replacing \(u\) by \(v^2u\), and the set \( \{ ut : u \in A\} \) is stable under \( \mathcal{O}^\times\)-conjugacy. The
\(\mathcal{O}^\times\)-orbit of \(ut\) is therefore
\(\{v^2ut:v\in \mathcal{O}^\times\}=(\mathcal{O}^\times)^2ut\). Hence \(ut\) and \(u't\) are
conjugate if and only if \(u'u^{-1}\in (\mathcal{O}^\times)^2\). This gives the bijection between conjugacy classes of elements \(ut\) and
\(\mathcal{O}^\times/(\mathcal{O}^\times)^2\).
